extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of Renaissance art; artists and art historians
extracted.subtask_description: Biographical/art-historical text (Vasari) that both narrates artists' lives and repeatedly evaluates works by criteria such as design, draughtsmanship, invention, finish, and technical mastery across painting, sculpture, and architecture. Useful for extracting period standards of good practice and judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drawing / Draughtsmanship
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘who drew very well for his time and for that manner… sheets of parchment drawn by his hand in water-colour, outlined with the pen’ — excellence of preparatory drawing and draughtsmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate, inventive draughtsmanship is a primary measure of skill; drawings in pen-and-wash or water-colour that show composition and line are prized evidence of an artist's mastery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chiaroscuro and use of highlights
rubrics_metrics.description: Works described as drawn ‘in chiaroscuro, with the high lights in white’ — modelling figures by light and shadow and using highlights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective modelling through light and shade (chiaroscuro) and judicious use of white highlights enhances volume and realism in drawing and painting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalism and lifelike detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote: Giotto ‘painted a fly on the nose of a figure… so true to nature that his master… set himself more than once to drive it away’ — fidelity to visible nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convincing, lifelike details (even minute ones) that deceive the eye are a sign of superior invention and observation from nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculptures praised as ‘the finest and best proportioned’ and paintings noted for ‘great invention and proportion’ — balanced arrangement and correct proportions of figures and elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmony of proportion and a well-ordered composition across figures, architecture and reliefs is central to judged excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colouring and tonal blending
rubrics_metrics.description: Stefano is said to be ‘more mellow, and better blended in colouring than all the others’ — superior handling of colour and transitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subtle, well-blended colouring and harmonious tones (rather than crude colouring) are markers of advanced painting technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention / Novelty (artistic innovation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as ‘he was the man who recovered the true method of painting’ and inventing ‘a new fashion of arms’ or ‘a flight of steps… so rich in design’ highlight invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New solutions of form, composition, technical devices, or a renewed method (recovering or improving earlier practice) are highly valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspective and architectural space
rubrics_metrics.description: Stefano ‘drew a building in perspective, perfectly and in a manner then little known’ — use of perspective to create coherent architectural space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate depiction of architectural space and use of perspective to situate figures and scenes convincingly is an important technical achievement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreshortening and anatomical depiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted foreshortenings: figures ‘with the arms, trunks, and legs foreshortened much better than any foreshortenings that had been made before’; also noted that early foreshortening could be ‘faulty’ yet pioneering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful foreshortening and convincing anatomy indicate advanced handling of form; early experimental attempts are praised even when imperfect because they lead progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workmanship, finish and diligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeated references to labour and time: artists ‘laboured eight whole years’, ‘endured very great fatigue’, and ‘put into it all diligence and study’ — quality tied to painstaking execution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thorough workmanship, careful finish, and evident industriousness (time and patience invested) are markers of the best works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative clarity and richness of scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of multi-scene tomb panels and altarpanels: ‘twelve scenes… with an infinite number of little figures… make a rich and beautiful adornment’ — clear storytelling and rich figural variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ability to render complex narratives clearly, with appropriate expressive attitudes and many small subsidiary figures that support the story, is a criterion of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of medium-specific techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: References to fresco, distemper panel, water-colour drawings, chasing in silver, enamel work, etc.: e.g. ‘a little panel in distemper… very well wrought’; ‘works wrought with the chasing-tool’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skill across the specific technical demands of each medium (fresco, panel, distemper, chasing/enamel, marble carving) is required; mastery in the chosen medium is evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sculptural relief, carving skill and finish
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for carved prophets and tombs: ‘carved some prophets in marble… the finest and best proportioned’; references to half-relief scenes and figures ‘one braccio and a half in height’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quality of relief carving, appropriate depth, modelling in marble, and the finish of small figures and ornamentation determine sculptural merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural design and civic utility
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributions of city works and engineering: ‘made the design of their Palace… Porta Romana… fountain… brought the waters… through pipes of lead and of clay’ and confining a river ‘with dykes and other most useful barriers’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Architects are judged both for aesthetic design (palaces, façades, gates) and for practical civic works (fountains, infrastructure, flood-control), showing technical/engineering competence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature, inscription and documented authorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Works bear inscriptions: e.g. carved words ‘HOC OPUS FECIT MAGISTER AUGUSTINUS ET MAGISTER ANGELUS DE SENIS.’ — marking authorship and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear marking, signatures, dates and inscriptions are important for attribution and for the reputation of the master; documented authorship is valued.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fulfilling commissions and asserting the value of work
rubrics_metrics.description: Giotto buckler anecdote: he painted an entire suit of armour on a client's buckler when asked to 'paint my arms', then defended his payment successfully in judgement — negotiating interpretation and value of the commission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarity in responding to a patron's brief, confidence in the artist's interpretation, and willingness to defend the labour and value of the work (including legally or socially) factor into professional judgement.
